title: Process optimization of extreme high-speed laser cladding: materials, parameters, external field assistance, and future trends
abstract: Abstract Extreme high-speed laser cladding (EHLC, Extreme High-Speed Laser Cladding) has attracted attention in material surface modification, due to its high energy density (3 kW/cm 2 ), high deposition rates (20–500 m/min), and notable coating performance. However, the rapid heating and cooling inherent to EHLC can introduce stress concentrations within the coating, resulting in defects such as cracks and porosity that may degrade performance. Process optimization is essential for minimizing these defects and advancing coating quality. This paper reviews current research in EHLC technology, beginning with an overview of its fundamental principles and criteria for cladding material selection, including powder characteristics. The effects of processing parameters, such as laser power, scanning speed, and overlap ratio, on coating quality are analyzed alongside established optimization methods. The influence of external field-assisted technologies on coating properties and their mechanisms for regulating microstructures have been discussed. Finally, future trends in EHLC optimization are identified, with the goal of supporting broader adoption in material modification.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: In contemporary manufacturing, the failure of mechanical components frequently originates at the surface or is associated with surface-related phenomena [ 1 ]. Investigating efficient and reliable surface repair technologies holds great significance and value for real-world applications. Hard chrome plating (HCP, Hard Chrome Plating) [ 2 ] technology has demonstrated significant effectiveness in enhancing the hardness, wear resistance, and corrosion resistance of components, leading to its widespread adoption. However, this technology has also contributed to increasingly severe environmental pollution problems, posing a major obstacle to its sustainable development [ 3 ]. Alternative coating technologies to HCP include thermal spray, overlay welding, and laser cladding. The thermal spray process is both versatile and user-friendly, making it suitable for extensive spraying on large components as well as localized applications in specific areas [ 4 ]. Nevertheless, the sprayed layer is mechanically bonded to the substrate, resulting in relatively low bonding strength and the presence of defects such as porosity [ 5 ]. In contrast, while overlay welding technology offers high bonding strength, its low productivity and limited range of compatible materials significantly restrict its applicability.

In comparison to other surface repair technologies, laser cladding has increasingly demonstrated significant potential for advancement in the surface repair sector, due to its ability to produce dense, minimally defective coatings that are metallurgically bonded to the substrate [ 6 ]. However, conventional laser cladding (CLC, Conventional Laser Cladding) technology often encounters difficulties in enhancing coating quality while simultaneously pursuing high cladding efficiency, posing a persistent challenge in this field's development [ 7 ]. To address these issues, the Fraunhofer Institute for Laser Technology and RWTH Aachen University collaboratively introduced EHLC technology, successfully developing the pertinent equipment in 2017 [ 8 ]. As a revolutionary alternative to traditional methods such as HCP, EHLC technology quickly garnered substantial interest following its introduction. The innovative feature of EHLC technology allows for the precise deposition of cladding materials in a liquid state onto the substrate surface by manipulating the laser beam's focal point, powder flow, and melt pool [ 9 ]. This advancement not only significantly reduces the duration of the melt pool, thereby enhancing cladding efficiency (CLC approximately 0.06 m 2 /h, EHLC up to 0.6 m 2 /h) and powder utilization rate (CLC approximately 60–80%, EHLC: 85–95%), but also further improves the microstructure and quality of the coating [ 10 ]. Consequently, it has emerged as an optimal solution for coating large-scale components [ 11 ].

Despite the remarkable advantages that EHLC technology offers in enhancing coating performance, it continues to encounter several technical challenges that must be addressed. As highlighted by Ding et al. [ 12 ], although Inconel 625 coatings produced through EHLC technology display superior surface quality and performance compared to those created via CLC, the accelerated cooling rate can lead to a non-uniform distribution of elements and microstructural characteristics within the coating, ultimately affecting its performance. Similarly, researchers such as Sun et al. [ 13 ] found that during the production of chromium-rich stainless steel coatings using EHLC technology, the rapid cooling rate impeded the complete transformation to martensite, resulting in a reduction in the coating's hardness. In addition, the high cooling rate of EHLC technology may cause cracks in brittle materials (such as high-carbon alloys or ceramics), and the rapid thermal cycling during the cladding process may generate significant residual stresses, which may affect the service life of the components. To address these issues, residual stresses must be controlled or eliminated through subsequent heat treatment or other process methods to improve the reliability and overall performance of the coating. These challenges emphasize the imperative for continued research in EHLC technology to focus on achieving uniformity in the coatings' microstructure while concurrently improving cladding efficiency, thus elevating the overall performance of the coatings.

In response to this, the present paper offers a systematic review of the optimization strategies for EHLC technology, grounded in a comprehensive elucidation of its fundamental principles. The discussion includes the selection of material systems, the optimization of processing parameters, the application of numerical simulation techniques, and the integrated use of various external field-assisted technologies (Any non-contact physical field used to condition the process, including but not limited to ultrasonic, thermal, magnetic, and electric fields.). Designed to offer practical guidance and theoretical support for researchers and engineering professionals in related fields, thereby fostering the ongoing advancement of EHLC technology.

sections.heading: EHLC technology
paragraphs: EHLC technology, recognized as an advanced laser surface modification technique, has emerged as a pivotal breakthrough in the field of material processing [ 14 ]. This technique utilizes a high-power laser beam to heat the substrate surface, allowing the cladding material and specific areas of the substrate to melt and fuse simultaneously, thereby producing a coating with unique performance characteristics [ 15 ]. Compared to CLC technology (material utilization rate: 60–80%), EHLC technology achieves a higher material utilization rate (85–95%) due to its optimized laser beam transmission system, fully demonstrating its outstanding technical advantages [ 16 ]. The cladding speed of EHLC technology typically ranges from 20 to 200 m/min, representing a significant improvement over CLC technology, which operates within a speed range of 0.2 to 0.8 m/min [ 17 ]. Such an enhancement in speed enables EHLC technology to undertake coating operations over larger areas within a shorter timeframe, thereby substantially boosting production efficiency. EHLC technology demonstrates a significant advantage in cladding efficiency (85–95%), with an efficiency approximately 1.4 times higher than CLC technology (60–75%) [ 18 ].

Figure  1  visually illustrates the schematic diagram illustrating the fundamental principles of CLC and EHLC technologies [ 19 ]. In EHLC technology, a substantial portion of the laser energy is directly directed toward the cladding powder, ensuring it attains a fully molten state before contact with the substrate [ 20 ]. This strategic distribution of energy not only significantly enhances the efficiency of cladding powder utilization but also minimizes thermal input to the substrate [ 21 ], thereby reducing the risk of deformation from excessive heating and further optimizing the quality and performance of the coating [ 22 ]. In contrast, CLC technology primarily employs laser energy to melt the substrate's surface rather than the cladding powder itself [ 23 ]. This energy distribution strategy may lead to an increased melting depth of the substrate, which in turn raises the dilution rate of the coating. An elevated dilution rate will profoundly impact the overall performance of the coating, especially its critical attributes, including hardness, corrosion, and wear resistance [ 24 ]. Fig. 1 Schematic diagram of the process principle:  a  CLC;  b  EHLC [ 19 ]

The immense potential of EHLC technology has been thoroughly validated through extensive academic research in specific application areas. Figure  2  meticulously outlines the primary advantages of EHLC technology and its distinct manifestations across various fields. For example, Tuominen et al. [ 25 ] from Tampere University observed in salt spray tests that nickel-based coatings produced via EHLC technology, characterized by low dilution rates, exhibited remarkable corrosion resistance, thereby effectively safeguarding the cast iron substrate. Furthermore, the research team discovered that nickel-based composite coatings with a hardness of 1200 HV demonstrated superior wear resistance compared to traditional hard chrome coatings in low-stress wear testing conditions. Bi et al. [ 26 ] from Tianjin University of Technology and Education undertook a comprehensive investigation into the application of EHLC technology for the surface modification of titanium alloys, particularly focusing on the development of high-temperature resistant alloy coatings. Their findings reveal that the Al 0.2 CrNbTiV alloy coating applied using EHLC technology significantly enhances the ablation resistance of titanium alloys. This research outcome holds considerable significance for prolonging the lifespan of titanium alloy components in high-temperature and complex operational environments. Fig. 2 EHLC technology advantages and application areas

It is important to emphasize that the core advantages of EHLC technology lie in micro-nano scale processing and thin coating preparation. Its extremely high deposition speed of 20–500 m/min, coupled with high material utilization rates of 85–95% and coating efficiency of 0.6 m 2 /h, enables exceptional performance in scenarios requiring high-precision, large-area thin coatings (such as aerospace components with stringent surface accuracy requirements). However, due to its extremely rapid cooling characteristics, EHLC must reduce cladding speed to ensure coating quality when preparing thicker protective layers (200–500 μm) [ 27 ]. In such cases, high-speed laser cladding (HLC) technology becomes a more suitable complementary solution.

The cladding speed of HLC technology ranges from 1 to 20 m/min, which is lower than EHLC but still significantly higher than CLC [ 28 ]. Material utilization reaches 75–85%, positioned between CLC (60–80%) and EHLC, achieving a balanced trade-off between efficiency and cost; cladding efficiency is 0.1–0.3 m 2 /h, precisely matching the requirements for preparing medium-thickness to thick coatings. For example, research conducted by Yu et al. [ 29 ] demonstrates that, under various wear conditions, the wear resistance of HLC coatings markedly surpasses that of CLC coatings. Consequently, HLC is particularly suited for traditional industrial applications requiring wear-resistant layers of 200–500 μm, such as in industrial machinery components.

In summary, EHLC and HLC technologies are not mutually exclusive but rather complementary based on the “coating thickness-performance requirement” relationship. EHLC technology stands out in micro-nano scale processing and high-performance coating production due to its rapid cladding speed [ 30 ]. Conversely, HLC technology offers robust stability and cost-effectiveness in thick coating manufacturing, making it well-suited for a diverse array of traditional industrial applications [ 31 ]. As these two technologies continue to evolve and improve, they will undoubtedly establish a more solid technological foundation for the flourishing development of modern manufacturing, enabling various industries to achieve substantial advancements in precision, efficiency, and functionality.

sections.heading: EHLC material system
paragraphs: In the selection of cladding materials, it is imperative to thoroughly assess their physicochemical compatibility and matching degree with the substrate, while also performing an in-depth analysis of the specific application requirements [ 32 ]. Establishing a stable and robust metallurgical bond interface between the cladding and the substrate, coupled with outstanding wear resistance, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature stability, is vital for improving coating quality and prolonging its service life [ 33 ]. Figure  3  offers a systematic overview of the primary categories of cladding materials based on their composition and characteristics, including alloy powders, ceramic powders, and composite powders. The main types of alloy powders consist of conventional alloy powders [ 34 ], self-fluxing alloy powders [ 35 ], medium/high-entropy alloy powders [ 36 ], and amorphous alloy powders [ 37 ]. Ceramic powders are favored for their remarkable wear resistance and high-temperature capabilities, such as aluminum oxide, silicon nitride, and silicon carbide [ 38 ]. Composite powders achieve superior performance by synergistically combining the advantages of diverse materials [ 39 ]. Moreover, to significantly improve the overall performance of the coatings, specialized functional additives, including self-lubricating phases [ 40 ], rare earth oxides [ 41 ], and carbon nanotubes [ 42 ], have been progressively integrated into the cladding material systems. Fig. 3 EHLC cladding material system

sections.heading: Alloy powders
paragraphs: Based on their composition and structural characteristics, alloy powders can primarily be classified into four categories: traditional alloy powders (e.g., Ni–Cr, Fe-Cu systems) consist of 1–2 main elements plus small amounts of alloying elements, featuring well-defined crystal structures and equilibrium phase diagrams; self-fluxing alloy powders (e.g., NiCrBSi) incorporate elements such as B/Si to form a liquid phase during heating, promoting densification; high/medium entropy alloy powders are composed of multiple main elements (≥ 3 isomolar elements), and their structures can range from single-phase solid solutions to complex intermetallic phases depending on processing conditions; amorphous alloy powders, on the other hand, achieve short-range ordered amorphous structures through rapid solidification. For example, Huang et al. [ 43 ] employed EHLC technology to fabricate CrFeCoNiMo 0.2  HEA coatings. The experimental results demonstrate that, in comparison to CLC coatings, EHLC coatings not only display markedly improved surface precision but also exhibit a significant refinement of the microstructure (as depicted in Fig.  4 ), which greatly enhances both the mechanical properties and corrosion resistance of the coatings. Fig. 4 Comparison of surface accuracy and grain size of CLC and EHLC coatings [ 43 ]

Similarly, the Inconel 625 coatings developed by Ding et al. [ 12 ] utilizing EHLC technology surpass those produced through CLC methods. Finite element simulation analysis revealed that, at identical locations, the maximum temperature of the EHLC coatings is considerably lower than that of the HLC coatings. This finding underscores the rapid heating and cooling characteristics inherent to EHLC technology, which are the primary contributors to the disparities in microstructure and performance between the two coating types [ 44 ]. Furthermore, research conducted by Wang et al. [ 45 ] indicates that EHLC technology can yield iron-based amorphous alloy coatings with a more homogeneous distribution of amorphous phases and a higher overall content, thereby enhancing coating performance. In conclusion, the elevated cooling rate associated with EHLC technology, resulting in microstructural refinement and uniform composition distribution, is a crucial factor in the substantial improvement of coating performance.

sections.heading: Ceramic powders
paragraphs: Ceramic powders are esteemed as the preferred materials for cladding due to their exceptional hardness. Nevertheless, significant disparities in thermophysical properties between ceramic powders and metal substrates frequently result in the emergence of cracks and pores within the coatings [ 46 ], presenting a critical challenge that necessitates resolution in practical applications. To address this challenge, Liu et al. [ 47 ] innovatively utilized HLC technology to successfully fabricate ZrB2-SiC continuous gradient composite coatings. This composite not only mitigates the incompatibility issues between metal and ceramic to a certain extent but also features a gradient in hardness that progressively increases from the substrate to the surface, achieved through the establishment of a gradient in microstructure and elemental distribution, as illustrated in Fig.  5 a~d. This gradient architecture not only enhances the overall performance of the coating but also significantly improves its durability in high-load and extreme environments. Fig. 5 a  Schematic distribution of microstructure gradients in the coating cross-section;  b  coating surface-to-substrate line scan analysis;  c  hardness cloud map of the coating cross-section; and ( d ) hardness indentation map from substrate to coating surface [ 47 ]

sections.heading: Composite powders
paragraphs: In addition to the preparation of ceramic coatings, another common method is to mix ceramic powders with metal powders to prepare a "metal + ceramic" composite powder. For instance, Li et al. [ 48 ] developed AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 -WC composite coatings with varying WC concentrations utilizing EHLC technology. Research indicates that as the WC content increases, the grain size of the coatings gradually refines, while the amounts of hard phases W 2 C and Cr 23 C 6  also rise, significantly enhancing the wear resistance of the coatings. The study by Hu et al. [ 49 ] corroborates this observation, confirming that WC serves as a beneficial reinforcing phase that positively influences the coating's performance. Furthermore, Du et al. [ 50 ] successfully fabricated (Ti, Nb)(C, B)/IN625 composite coatings by integrating EHLC with in-situ synthesis techniques, achieving notable friction reduction and enhanced wear resistance. This research suggests that the incorporation of reinforcing phases via in-situ synthesis can substantially improve the overall performance of the coatings. However, mechanically mixed composite powders often face challenges such as low bonding strength and interfacial cracking during the cladding process. To address these challenges, Zhou et al. [ 51 ] employed a hydrothermal hydrogen reduction method to produce Ti 2 AlC@Ni core–shell composite powders. HLC experiments demonstrate that this composite powder can form metallurgical bonded cladding layers with no significant defects and uniform dispersion of strengthening phases, as shown in Fig.  6 a~f. The synergistic effect of this defect-free structure and uniform strengthening phase distribution effectively enhances the overall performance of the coating. Fig. 6 Cross-sectional morphology of Ni-based cermet coating:  a  overall morphology,  b  backscattered electron imaging of overall morphology,  c  local magnification,  d  microstructure at the bottom of the coating,  e  microstructure in the middle of the coating,  f  microstructure at the top of the coating [ 51 ]

sections.heading: Additives
paragraphs: To enhance the overall performance of the cladding layer, one might consider incorporating functional additives such as self-lubricating phases, rare earth oxides, and carbon nanotubes. For example, Yu et al. [ 52 ] examined the effect of cBN on the properties of the (CoCrNi) 88 Al 6 Ti 6  coatings, revealing that during the high-temperature laser cladding process, a portion of cBN is transformed into hBN, which markedly improves the wear resistance of the coating through the synergistic effects of various strengthening mechanisms. Lin et al. [ 53 ] identified that Y 2 O 3  can refine the grain structure of the IN718 coating, fortify the grain boundaries, diminish impurities, reduce crack sensitivity, and enhance resistance to high-temperature corrosion. Figure  7 a presents a comparative schematic depicting the coating grain structure and corrosion mechanisms before and following the incorporation of Y 2 O 3 . Without Y₂O₃ addition, the coating exhibits coarse grains and numerous defects. During high-temperature corrosion, the oxide layer becomes loose and prone to flaking, resulting in significant chromium loss. Upon adding 1.0 wt% Y₂O₃, new nucleation sites form at grain boundaries due to Y₂O₃. This leads to grain refinement and reduced defects, forming a dense Cr₂O₃ oxide layer on the surface. Consequently, high-temperature corrosion resistance is significantly enhanced. Fig. 7 a  Comparison of coating grain and corrosion mechanism before and after the addition of Y 2 O 3  [ 53 ];  b  Schematic diagram of frictional corrosion mechanism of coatings with different graphene contents [ 54 ]

Yuan et al. [ 55 ] investigated the impact of nickel-plated carbon nanotubes as additives in Fe-based amorphous coatings, concluding that while an increase in additive content corresponds with a decrease in the amorphous phase and microhardness, the coatings exhibited marked improvements in self-lubricating properties, wear resistance, and corrosion resistance. Furthermore, Yu et al. [ 54 ] explored the effect of graphene content on the performance of CoCrFeMo HEA coatings, noting that the combined effects of the carbide-reinforced phase and the self-lubricating properties of graphene significantly enhance both corrosion resistance and friction performance of the coatings. Figure  7 b depicts a schematic representation of the corrosion wear mechanism for coatings with different graphene concentrations. Without graphene (HEA-G0), fatigue wear and corrosion wear dominate, leading to coating delamination. At low content levels (1.5 wt%, 2.5 wt%), the wear mechanism involves abrasive + corrosion wear, where TiC reinforcement and self-lubricating properties enhance performance. At high content levels (3.5 wt%, 4 wt%), graphene agglomeration induces adhesive wear, deepening grooves and exacerbating corrosion pitting and spalling, leading to degraded coating performance. In EHLC, although additive powders can enhance coating performance, cost-effectiveness must be carefully balanced. For example, carbon nanotubes are expensive and require complex dispersion processes, which may increase production costs; graphite, on the other hand, is less expensive and easier to scale up, but offers limited performance improvements. In industrial production, material selection must be based on specific requirements, and deposition efficiency can be enhanced by optimizing process parameters such as powder feed rate and laser power. Additionally, the development of low-cost, high-stability powder supply systems is necessary to enable large-scale application.

To systematically demonstrate the compatibility and performance characteristics of different cladding materials with the EHLC process, Table  1  summarizes the core parameters and key performance data for the alloy powders, ceramic powders, composite powders, and functional additives discussed in this paper. Overall, alloy powders exhibit remarkable potential for application in laser cladding technology, especially through comprehensive investigations into medium and high-entropy alloys, as well as amorphous alloys. These studies not only significantly broaden the range of cladding materials but also pave the way for new research opportunities aimed at enhancing coating performance [ 57 ]. Moreover, gradient composite coatings developed via EHLC technology [ 58 ] offer an effective solution for ensuring robust adhesion between ceramic powders and metal substrates, highlighting their substantial application potential. By skillfully integrating composite powder technology with both ceramic and metal powders, and by incorporating functional components such as self-lubricating phases, rare earth oxides, and carbon nanotubes, one can significantly improve the mechanical properties and corrosion resistance of the cladding layer [ 59 ,  60 – 61 ]. Nonetheless, it is imperative to meticulously regulate various process parameters during the EHLC procedure to mitigate the risk of crack formation, particularly when the content of ceramic powders is elevated.

sections.heading: Optimization of EHLC process parameters
paragraphs: Figure  8  depicts the essential parameters involved in the EHLC process and their principal effects on the properties of the cladding layer. These process parameters are interdependent rather than independent. Specifically, laser power (P), spot diameter (D), and scanning speed (V) jointly determine the laser energy density (P/D × V) during the cladding process [ 62 ], which directly affects the heat input to the substrate. Effective control of heat input is vital, as it is closely linked to the dilution rate of the coating. A high dilution rate can lead to a decline in coating performance, particularly evident in the reduction of critical properties such as hardness, toughness, and corrosion resistance [ 63 ]. Furthermore, the powder feed rate and overlap rate, as additional crucial parameters, significantly influence the macro morphology of the coating. The powder feed rate dictates the quantity of cladding material supplied per unit time, thereby impacting the thickness and uniformity of the coating [ 64 ]; meanwhile, the overlap rate pertains to the extent of overlap between various cladding paths, which directly affects the surface precision of the coating [ 65 ]. Fig. 8 Key EHLC parameters and their main effects on the properties of the cladding layer

To achieve high-quality and high-performance coatings, extensive research has been undertaken by numerous scholars to optimize the process parameters of EHLC technology. For example, investigations by Yang et al. [ 66 ], Chen et al. [ 67 ], and Shen et al. [ 24 ] demonstrate that an increase in scanning speed effectively facilitates the refinement of coating grains, ensures a uniform distribution of elements, and significantly diminishes the coating thickness, the depth of heat-affected zone, and the dilution rate, as depicted in Fig.  9 a~d. These phenomena are intrinsically linked to the high cooling rate characteristic of EHLC technology and its distinctive light-powder coupling mechanism. Yan et al. [ 68 ] explored the influence of varying overlap rates on the surface roughness of EHLC coatings. Their findings reveal that a markedly low overlap rate results in pronounced overlap marks on the coating surface and inadequate coating thickness, hindering the formation of an effective protective barrier, which may consequently compromise the coating's lifespan and overall performance. Conversely, when the overlap rate is excessively high, although the overlap marks on the coating surface vanish, sintering phenomena and indentation defects may occur, as illustrated in Fig.  9 e, which similarly detrimentally impacts the overall performance of the coating. Fig. 9 a ~ d  Cross-sectional morphology of coatings at different scanning speeds [ 67 ];  e  Surface morphology of coatings with different overlap rates [ 68 ]

The research conducted by Chen et al. [ 69 ] revealed that, with increasing laser power, the hardness of the FeCrBSi coating initially decreases before subsequently rising. This phenomenon can be attributed to a decrease in the amorphous phase content and an increase in grain size due to enhanced laser power, which simultaneously facilitates the formation of intermetallic compounds. Huang et al. [ 43 ] underscored the necessity of maintaining laser power within a judicious range in EHLC technology, as both excessively high and low power levels can negatively impact the coating. Concurrently, Wu et al. [ 70 ] explored the influences of laser energy density and defocus on the characteristics of EHLC coatings, asserting that energy density is a pivotal factor in determining coating thickness, microstructure, and overall performance. Specifically, insufficient energy density may lead to inadequate melting, resulting in subpar coating thickness; conversely, excessive energy density can induce overheating, causing burning or deformation that adversely affects coating performance. Additionally, variations in defocus amount directly affect the laser energy applied to the powder above the substrate, thereby affecting both the thickness and uniformity of the coating.

Tan et al. [ 56 ] explored the impact of WC particle size on the microstructure and wear resistance of Ni/WC composite coatings. Their findings revealed that tungsten carbide particles of different sizes significantly influence the wear resistance of composite coatings by affecting grain growth mechanisms and microstructure. When small-sized WC particles are uniformly distributed, they effectively refine grain size and enhance second-phase strengthening, thereby improving coating hardness and wear resistance; medium-sized particles cause disordered dendritic grain growth directions due to local aggregation, resulting in a slight decrease in wear resistance; large-sized particles have poor dispersion, limited grain refinement effects, and exhibit the weakest wear resistance. Therefore, compared to other coatings, small-particle WC coatings demonstrate the best wear resistance due to grain refinement strengthening and uniform distribution of the strengthening phase. Figure  10  depicts the mechanisms of grain growth within the composite coating under different WC particle size conditions. 30–65 μm: WC particles exhibit uniform dispersion with slight decomposition, enhancing nucleation rate and inhibiting dendrite growth to achieve grain refinement. 65–100 μm: WC particles readily agglomerate, causing disordered growth orientation in intermediate columnar grains. 100–145 μm: Large WC particles exhibit poor dispersion, concentrating in the upper coating region and diminishing their grain refinement effect on the substrate. Grain size decreases along the growth direction. Fig. 10 Growth mechanisms of grains around WC particles of different sizes:  a  30–65 μm;  b  65–100 μm;  a  100–145 μm [ 56 ]

In conclusion, the influence of various cladding materials and process parameters on coating performance is multifaceted, and the rational selection of process parameters is crucial for ensuring coating quality [ 71 ]. Table  2  summarizes the effects of core process parameters on coating quality and performance, listing the optimal parameter ranges obtained from existing optimization studies. This table establishes quantitative relationships between parameters and performance, providing direct technical references for practical applications. While univariate optimization methods can effectively illustrate the effects of individual laser cladding parameters on cladding outcomes—thus streamlining experimental design and minimizing costs—this methodology may neglect potential interactions between parameters and show low optimization efficiency. Consequently, it is imperative to develop more sophisticated and universally applicable approaches for optimizing process parameters. At present, the predominant methods for process parameter optimization, both nationally and internationally, encompass experimental optimization methods, intelligent algorithms, and numerical simulation methodologies.

sections.heading: Experimental optimization methods
paragraphs: Experimental optimization methods represent a holistic approach that combines experimental design strategies—such as orthogonal, Taguchi, and uniform design methods—with mathematical analytical techniques, including range analysis, fuzzy evaluation, and grey relational analysis [ 73 ], and they are widely applied in the field of process parameter optimization. Notably, they are distinguished by their intuitive nature and operational simplicity, demonstrating significant advantages in addressing multi-level process parameter optimization issues.

For example, Wang et al. [ 74 ] performed parameter optimization for a single-layer cladding of the EHLC K648 high-temperature alloy utilizing an orthogonal experimental design. Through variance analysis, they discerned that the powder feed rate, laser power, and scanning speed were the most critical factors influencing the width, height, and depth of the single-layer cladding, respectively. They determined the optimal combination of process parameters with the primary goals of suitably enhancing the cladding width and height, judiciously reducing the depth, and minimizing defects. The resulting cladding layer demonstrated exceptional internal quality, with no discernible crack defects observed, as depicted in Fig.  11 a. Fig. 11 a  Metallographic morphology of K648 coating cross-section under optimal process parameters [ 74 ];  b  Evaluation flow of AHP-FCE method [ 75 ];  b  Plot of predicted versus actual values for single-pass width;  c  Scanning speed versus powder feed rate, ( d ) laser power versus powder feed rate, and ( e ) laser power versus scanning speed 3D response surface plots [ 68 ]

Xv et al. [ 75 ] employed the Taguchi method as an experimental design approach to optimize the process parameters for Fe–Cr-Ni-based coatings fabricated on ASTM 1045 steel. They adeptly integrated the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) with the Fuzzy Comprehensive Evaluation (FCE) model, thereby transforming the multi-objective quality evaluation challenge into a single-objective optimization problem grounded in the weights of the criterion layers. Figure  11 b depicts the evaluation framework of the AHP-FCE method. This strategy effectively minimized the impact of subjective human factors and ensured data consistency, thereby providing a robust foundation for the quality assessment of Fe–Cr-Ni-based cladding layers and the optimization of process parameters.

Furthermore, Yong et al. [ 76 ] established a predictive model for the relationship between process parameters and cladding layer height and Vickers hardness using Response Surface Methodology (RSM), validating the model's predictive accuracy through experimental data. Concurrently, Yan et al. [ 68 ] utilized RSM to explore the influence of laser power, scanning speed, and powder feed rate on the width of a single-pass cladding layer, thereby providing a theoretical foundation for the further optimization of the coating overlap ratio. Figure  11 c~f illustrates a comparison of the predicted and actual measurements of coating width, along with the 3D response surface plots depicting the relationship between process parameters and response objectives.

In summary, experimental optimization methods effectively address multi-level process parameter optimization challenges by integrating experimental design with mathematical analysis [ 77 ]. However, this approach depends on laboratory experiments, requiring systematic adjustments of process parameters and careful observation of their effects on coating performance to determine optimal conditions. While it can provide direct and reliable experimental data, this method often demands significant time and resources and may not thoroughly explore all combinations of parameters. Consequently, in practical applications, combining this method with other optimization techniques, such as intelligent optimization or numerical simulation, may produce more favorable results.

sections.heading: Intelligent algorithms
paragraphs: Intelligent algorithms, with their ability to develop high-precision mathematical models, can adeptly analyze extensive experimental datasets [ 78 ], thus facilitating a comprehensive investigation into the intricate nonlinear relationships between process parameters and the quality of the cladding layer [ 79 ].

Xv et al. [ 19 ] conducted a comparative analysis of the predictive accuracy of two models developed using Random Forest (RF) and AdaBoost (AB) algorithms, as illustrated in detail in Fig.  12 a-b. Their findings reveal that the AB-based predictive model exhibited superior accuracy relative to the RF model. Furthermore, the analysis highlighted scanning speed as a pivotal factor influencing both the height of the coating and its surface roughness. Additionally, the overlap ratio was validated as an essential parameter for effectively managing the coating dilution rate and the grain size near the surface. Concurrently, the interplay between laser power and scanning speed had a significant impact on the thermal input and microhardness of the substrate. These research findings provide a solid scientific foundation for the subsequent optimization and adjustment of cladding process parameters. Fig. 12 Prediction model prediction process:  a  RF model [ 19 ];  b  AB model [ 79 ];  c  GRNN-NSGA-II optimization process [ 80 ]

Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) [ 81 ], particularly Back Propagation (BP) neural networks [ 82 ] and genetic algorithm-optimized BP (GABP) neural networks [ 83 ], have seen extensive application in the optimization of process parameters. In the EHLC process, multi-objective optimization of these parameters is frequently accomplished by integrating modeling techniques—such as RSM and BPNN—with metaheuristic algorithms, including Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) [ 84 ] and the second-generation Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm (NSGA-II) [ 85 ]. For instance, Zhang et al. [ 80 ] optimized the process parameters for laser cladding of CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy coatings using a synergistic approach that combines Generalized Regression Neural Networks (GRNN) with NSGA-II, as depicted in Fig.  12 c. The findings reveal that the relative error between the optimized actual values and the predicted values remained within 10%. Moreover, a comprehensive analysis of the microstructure and wear resistance of the coatings substantiated the efficacy and reliability of this optimization strategy. This research offers valuable insights and effective methodologies for the optimization of EHLC process parameters.

In future EHLC applications, machine learning will demonstrate vast potential [ 86 ] :  by leveraging neural networks to analyze multi-modal sensor data (such as melt pool images, thermal fields, and spectra) in real time, it enables millisecond-level detection of process anomalies; by combining reinforcement learning to dynamically optimize parameters such as laser power and scanning speed, it forms an adaptive closed-loop control system; and by integrating digital twins with physical models, it achieves high-precision prediction of forming quality and process calibration. Machine learning not only significantly enhances cladding efficiency and defect suppression capabilities but also adapts to new materials and scenarios through cross-scale modeling and online learning, driving the transition of laser additive manufacturing toward autonomy and intelligence [ 87 ].

As artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies continue to evolve, intelligent optimization algorithms have emerged as essential instruments in the domain of parameter optimization. These algorithms harness their profound analytical capabilities to navigate large datasets, effectively uncovering optimal solutions within intricate parameter landscapes, and demonstrating particular proficiency in managing nonlinear complex relationships [ 88 ]. It is crucial to acknowledge that the quality and scale of the data, alongside the choice of intelligent optimization algorithms and their parameter configurations, significantly influence the efficacy of the optimization outcomes. Furthermore, the decision-making processes inherent in these algorithms often exhibit a "black box" nature, which somewhat constrains their applicability in specific contexts.

sections.heading: Numerical simulation methodologies
paragraphs: In the realm of coating quality prediction and optimization, numerical simulation technology is esteemed for its remarkable simulation capabilities [ 89 ]. This technology adeptly models the dynamic behavior of the molten pool and the phase transformation processes while elucidating the evolution patterns of temperature and stress fields [ 90 ]. Such insights are essential for a comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms governing the cladding process, offering a robust theoretical foundation and substantial support for the optimization of process parameters.

The research conducted by Li et al. [ 72 ] compellingly illustrates the remarkable capabilities of numerical simulation technology in the prediction and optimization of coating quality. They utilized finite element analysis to investigate the distribution characteristics of temperature and stress fields, as well as the deformation of NiTi coatings fabricated under varying EHLC laser power conditions, as depicted in Fig.  13 . The findings reveal that an increase in laser power significantly enlarges the molten pool, resulting in heightened coating deformation. This phenomenon is primarily ascribed to the rapid volumetric changes (expansion and contraction) of the molten pool during the melting and solidification phases, leading to a substantial concentration of equivalent residual stress within both the molten pool and its heat-affected zone, which markedly affects the quality and performance of the coating. Conversely, Wei et al. [ 91 ] conducted a comprehensive systematic analysis of the effects of various process parameters on crack initiation and propagation behavior by integrating numerical simulations with experimental validation, ultimately identifying the optimized combination of process parameters. Fig. 13 Temperature field, deformation, longitudinal stress field, and transverse residual stress distribution of coatings at different laser powers:  a  2200 W,  b  2600 W,  c  3000 W,  d  3400 W,  e  3800 W [ 72 ]

When employing EHLC technology for the surface modification of cylindrical components, the volumetric effects of the substrate and its rotational motion can profoundly impact the EHLC process. Consequently, the development of a numerical model specifically designed for cylindrical substrates is of considerable practical significance. To validate the accuracy of the cylindrical model constructed (illustrated in Fig.  14 a), Lv et al. [ 20 ] compared experimental data with the depth of the heat-affected zone derived from numerical simulations, discovering that the discrepancy between the two was less than 14%. The researchers speculated that this error might be attributed to the model's inadequate consideration of the molten pool's fluid dynamics, as well as the challenges in precisely defining the heat-affected zone and substrate interface under an optical microscope. Fig. 14 a  Schematic diagram of the cylindrical model and its grid distribution [ 20 ];  b  Comparison of the actual melt pool contour and the melt pool contour simulated by different heat source models [ 92 ];  c  and  d  Comparison of real-time images and simulation results of powder convergence behaviour under different carrier gas flow rates and different powder feeding rates [ 93 ]

To further enhance predictive accuracy, Li et al. [ 92 ] innovatively proposed a combined heat source model, which was experimentally validated and demonstrated improved predictive performance (as depicted in Fig.  14 b). Furthermore, Zhang et al. [ 93 ] carried out research on the flow characteristics of Fe-based powders in the EHLC process using an annular nozzle powder flow model, validating their findings with high-speed camera technology (as shown in Fig.  14 c~d). Concurrently, they explored the effects of laser power and airflow on powder melting efficiency, thereby identifying the optimal combination of process parameters.

Numerical simulation technology facilitates a comprehensive analysis of the effect of various process parameters on the formation of the cladding layer [ 94 ]. By leveraging simulation results, researchers can not only anticipate the microstructure and macro performance of the coating, thereby optimizing the process parameters [ 95 ], but also perform preliminary parameter screening before conducting experiments, significantly reducing both the number of trials and associated costs. It is crucial to acknowledge that the accuracy of these simulation outcomes is heavily reliant on the validity of the constructed models and the precision of the input data.

In conclusion, each of these three optimization strategies possesses distinct characteristics. Experimental optimization methods are simple and straightforward but time-consuming and labor-intensive, and it is difficult to cover all parameter combinations. Intelligent optimization methods are suitable for handling nonlinear relationships but depend on the selection of algorithm parameters. Numerical simulation technology can save costs and predict performance [ 96 ], but its accuracy depends on the model and input data. Depending on the application scenario and requirements, we can combine multiple optimization methods to achieve better optimization results. Specifically, one might begin by employing simulation technology to define a preliminary range of process parameters, followed by further refinement through intelligent algorithms. Alternatively, the integration of machine learning algorithms with simulation technology can yield a more efficient optimization process.

sections.heading: EHLC external field-assisted optimization process
paragraphs: The selection of appropriate cladding materials and the optimization of process parameters can significantly mitigate the prevalence of defects within the coating. However, for cladding materials that exhibit high sensitivity to cracking, the EHLC process—characterized by its rapid cooling rates and overlap characteristics—can substantially elevate the average stress within the coating [ 97 ]. Consequently, even with the aforementioned optimization strategies, completely preventing the emergence of crack defects remains a formidable challenge. Additionally, the swift heating and cooling dynamics inherent in EHLC technology may result in inadequate element diffusion within the molten pool, adversely affecting the uniformity of the cladding layer's microstructure and ultimately compromising its overall performance [ 98 ]. In response to these challenges, researchers have actively pursued suitable composite processing techniques in recent years, striving to achieve a more uniform temperature field, stress distribution, and elemental composition through precise control of the convective dynamics of the molten pool.

sections.heading: Ultrasonic rolling-assisted EHLC technology
paragraphs: Ultrasonic rolling processing (USRP, Ultrasonic Surface Rolling Process) assisted EHLC technology by applying high-frequency impact grinding to the coating surface using an ultrasonic rolling head; the microstructure and surface properties of the coating are significantly improved [ 99 ]. The cavitation effects and dynamic impact forces generated by ultrasonic vibrations promote the fragmentation of dendrites within the melt pool, increase nucleation sites, and induce dislocation proliferation and dynamic recrystallization, thereby refining grain size and forming a uniform, fine, equiaxed grain structure. Concurrently, the plastic deformation caused by mechanical rolling effectively flattens surface irregularities, significantly reducing surface roughness. Furthermore, this technology introduces beneficial compressive stress onto the coating surface, counteracting part of the harmful tensile stress, thereby further optimizing material performance [ 100 ]. In terms of crack inhibition, ultrasonic vibration drives dislocation rearrangement, forming low-energy dislocation walls to alleviate local stress concentration, and releases residual stress through promoting grain boundary sliding and dynamic recovery; simultaneously, the refined grain boundary structure effectively blocks crack propagation paths, significantly enhancing the coating's crack resistance and service life [ 101 ]. Figure  15  depicts the structural diagram of the USRP implementation device [ 102 ] along with its operational principles [ 103 ]. Fig. 15 Ultrasonic surface rolling process:  a  Schematic diagram of the device [ 102 ];  b  Schematic diagram of the process principle [ 103 ]

Hao et al. [ 103 ], Chen et al. [ 104 ], Cui et al. [ 105 ], and Zhang et al. [ 106 ] each investigated the effects of USRP technology on the microstructures and properties of various alloy coatings. The findings of these studies consistently indicate that, following USRP treatment, the surface roughness of the coatings is obviously reduced, the grain structure is refined, and a uniform plastic deformation layer is established at the coating's surface, as depicted in Fig.  16 a~g. Significantly, the USRP treatment effectively transforms the residual tensile stresses inherent in the coating into advantageous compressive stress states. This alteration markedly improves the coating's hardness, wear resistance, and corrosion resistance, as illustrated in Fig.  16 h~j. Notably, the surface of the USRP-treated coating forms a denser oxide layer, which further amplifies its protective capabilities, enabling it to deliver exceptional performance in the face of complex environmental challenges. Fig. 16 a ~ c  Surface profile and top morphology of FeCoNiCrMn coating after USRP treatment;  d  Comparison of XRD spectra before and after USRP treatment [ 105 ];  e ~ f  Comparison of the surface of Fe-based coating before and after USRP treatment [ 106 ];  h ~ i  Comparison of the cross-sectional hardness, residual stresses, as well as the coefficient of friction and the amount of wear of Fe-based coating before and after USRP treatment [ 104 ]

sections.heading: Induction heating-assisted EHLC technology
paragraphs: The electromagnetic heating-assisted EHLC cladding (EH-LIHC, Extreme High-Speed Laser-Induction Hybrid Cladding) technology first raises the substrate surface temperature through induction heating [ 107 ], subsequently enabling the swift deposition of cladding material onto the surface using EHLC technology. This integrated approach not only ensures uniform heating of both the substrate and cladding material but also effectively diminishes the temperature gradient, thereby reducing residual stresses within the coating and mitigating the risk of cracking [ 108 ]. Figure  17  depicts the EH-LIHC process, which is equipped with an induction heater and monitoring system [ 109 ]. Fig. 17 Schematic diagram of the EHLC process with induction heater and monitoring system [ 109 ]

Researchers Li et al. [ 110 ] demonstrated that EH-LIHC technology offers significant advantages over traditional EHLC technology in the preparation of Ni60 coatings, notably by minimizing crack formation and achieving superior coating performance, as illustrated in Fig.  18 a. Furthermore, Li et al. [ 111 ] conducted a comparative analysis between EH-LIHC and conventional laser-induced hybrid cladding technology (LIHC). The findings reveal that Ni60 coatings produced via EH-LIHC exhibit reduced surface roughness, lower dilution rates, and enhanced deposition efficiency compared to those generated by LIHC, as depicted in Fig.  18 b. These results underscore the considerable potential of EH-LIHC technology in improving coating quality and production efficiency. Additionally, Li et al. [ 112 ] employed EH-LIHC technology to fabricate Ni60-WC composite coatings with varying WC content. Experimental results indicated that all composite coatings displayed lower surface roughness, with WC particles evenly distributed throughout the coatings. This further corroborates the reliability and efficacy of EH-LIHC technology in the production of high-performance composite coatings. Fig. 18 a  Surface macroscopic morphology of Ni60 coatings with crack detection under different process parameters [ 110 ];  b  Cross-sectional morphology of Ni60 coatings with different processes, comparison of dilution rate and melting rate [ 111 ]

sections.heading: Laser remelting
paragraphs: The essence of laser remelting (LR, Laser Remelting) technology lies in the use of a laser beam for irradiation, enabling a rapid melting and solidification process of the material's surface without the introduction of additional materials [ 113 ]. This technology not only effectively eliminates inherent defects within the material and promotes the uniformity of its microstructure but also substantially improves the material's hardness, wear resistance, and corrosion resistance through mechanisms such as quenching and recrystallization [ 114 ]. Figure  19  illustrates a comparative diagram of the principles underlying the EHLC and EHLC-LR processes [ 115 ]. Fig. 19 a  EHLC process schematic;  b  EHLC-LR process schematic [ 115 ]

For example, An et al. [ 116 ] conducted a comprehensive analysis through the development of a finite element model, revealing that a reduction in remelting speed not only increases the thermal input of the coating but also enhances the convective effects within the melt pool. This effectively diminishes defects while improving both the hardness and corrosion resistance of the coating. Similarly, Ding et al. [ 12 ] explored the impact of varying remelting power on the performance of EHLC coatings. Their findings indicated that elevated remelting power enhances the fluidity of the melt pool and promotes the uniform distribution of elements throughout the coating, thereby augmenting its wear resistance, as depicted in Fig.  20 a~d. Furthermore, Liu et al. [ 117 ] successfully fabricated a gradient-structured Fe 82 Cr 16 SiB alloy coating on an H13 steel substrate utilizing this integrated process. Their results demonstrated a significant reduction in surface roughness and a refinement in grain size following remelting treatment, as illustrated in Fig.  20 e~k. This microstructural refinement markedly improved both the wear and corrosion resistance of the coating. The findings of Xu et al. [ 115 ] further corroborate this conclusion. Fig. 20 a ~ d  EPMA plots of the surface principal element distribution of Inconel 625 coatings after wear testing at different remelting powers [ 12 ];  e  and  f  comparison of the surface morphology of the EHLC and EHLC-LR coatings;  g  XRD spectra of the EHLC and EHLC-LR coatings;  h ~ i  optical microstructures of the EHLC-LR coatings;  j  Comparison of microstructures of EHLC and EHLC-LR coatings in the near surface area region [ 117 ]

Expanding on this, Zhang et al. [ 118 ] discovered that the integration of EHLC with multiple laser remelting techniques not only markedly diminishes the surface roughness of the coating and refines its microstructure but also imparts advantageous features, including low-angle grain boundaries, a high-density of dislocations, and residual compressive stress. The synergistic effects of these characteristics substantially enhance the high-temperature corrosion resistance of the AlCoCrFeNi 2.1  coating, thereby opening new avenues for the application of EHLC technology in demanding environments characterized by elevated temperatures and corrosive conditions.

sections.heading: Heat treatment processes
paragraphs: Heat treatment (HT, Heat Treatment), a conventional materials processing technique, involves a series of heating, soaking, and cooling processes in designated media [ 119 ], to optimize material performance through the adjustment of its microstructure. In the context of EHLC coatings, subsequent heat treatment can effectively mitigate or eliminate compositional segregation and reduce residual stress levels, thereby significantly enhancing the overall performance of these coatings [ 120 ].

Currently, numerous researchers have undertaken various heat treatment processes to systematically explore their potential effects on the microstructure and performance of coatings. Li et al. [ 92 ] discovered that annealing treatment facilitates the growth of the oxide film on the surface of NiTi coatings, significantly enhancing their corrosion resistance. Research conducted by Dong et al. [ 121 ] reveals that as the annealing temperature gradually increases, the grain size of the Ni/316L coatings initially decreases before subsequently increasing, alongside a rise in the number of equiaxed grains and precipitates. This alteration in microstructure exerts a dual influence on the corrosion resistance of the coatings, initially improving it and later reducing it. Furthermore, Li et al. [ 122 ] innovatively introduced post-processing techniques such as power spinning (PS, Power Spinning) and post-spinning heat treatment (PSHT, Post-Spinning Heat Treatment), demonstrating that both PS and PSHT can enhance the wear resistance of the coatings. Specifically, PS refines the surface grains and promotes their directional alignment; with the application of HT, the coating’s microstructure is further optimized, resulting in a uniform dendritic eutectic structure, as illustrated in Fig.  21 a~h. This culminates in a denser coating with reduced dislocation density, thereby achieving improved wear resistance. Fig. 21 a  and  e  HLC coating grain vs. recrystallisation plots;  b  and  f  PS coating grain vs. recrystallisation plots;  c  and  g  PSHT coating grain vs. recrystallisation plots;  d  grain map statistics;  h  recrystallisation map statistics [ 122 ];  i  SEM images of unheat-treated coatings;  j  950 °C−1 h coating SEM image; (k1 ~ k2): 950 °C−2 h coating SEM images; (l1 ~ l3): 950 °C−3 h coating SEM images [ 123 ]

The study conducted by Wang et al. [ 123 ] examines the influence of high-temperature heat treatment duration on the corrosion resistance of Fe-based alloy coatings. The findings reveal that as the heat treatment duration is extended, internal stresses within the Fe-based alloy coatings are progressively alleviated, lattice distortion is minimized, dislocation density is reduced, and carbide content exhibits an increasing trend, as depicted in Fig.  21 i~l. Additionally, the activity and diffusion capacity of the chromium element is enhanced, promoting the development of a dense passivation film, which consequently augments the corrosion resistance of the coatings. Wang et al. [ 124 ] further explored the influence of different cooling rates on the mechanical properties of K648 high-temperature alloy coatings. The research indicates that a reduction in cooling rate results in grain coarsening within the coatings, alongside an increase in the sizes of carbides and α-Cr, accompanied by morphological alterations. This sequence of changes leads to improvements in hardness, tensile strength, and yield strength of the coatings; however, there is a notable decrease in elongation, primarily attributable to the direct influence of grain size variation on the material's plasticity.

In conclusion, optimizing the EHLC process through external field-assisted technology can markedly improve the overall performance of coatings, enabling them to better meet the demands of complex and dynamic environments. This approach lays a theoretical and practical foundation for the promotion and implementation of EHLC technology. Although external field-assisted EHLC technology can improve cladding quality, it also faces numerous limitations. The introduction of other fields, such as electromagnetic fields and ultrasonic fields, requires precise control of parameters, which increases process complexity and cost; simultaneously, energy loss and heat accumulation may reduce the effectiveness of the assistance. Additionally, the development of specialized equipment and high-load operation may impact stability and flexibility, while high costs and challenges in processing large workpieces hinder industrial applications. In the future, these limitations can be overcome through multi-field optimization, intelligent control algorithms, and novel field source designs.

sections.heading: Discussion and summary
paragraphs: A comprehensive review of EHLC technology reveals significant progress and challenges in several areas, including material systems, process parameter optimization, and external field-assisted techniques. The selection of alloy/ceramic/composite powders determines coating performance; self-lubricating phases and rare earth oxides enhance wear and corrosion resistance. Controlling cracks and porosity defects in high-ceramic-content coatings remains challenging, requiring precise regulation of process parameters. Laser power, scanning speed, and overlap rate influence coating quality and performance. Experimental optimization (orthogonal, Taguchi) offers intuitive insights but requires extensive testing; intelligent algorithms (neural networks, genetic algorithms) combined with numerical simulation deliver high efficiency and precision but necessitate robust data and model support. A hybrid strategy represents the optimal approach. Techniques such as ultrasonic rolling improve microstructural uniformity, reduce residual stresses, and enhance performance, addressing cooling and thermal gradient issues in EHLC. However, these methods increase process complexity and cost. Future optimization of this process will require multi-field coupling and intelligent control.

sections.heading: Conclusion and outlook
paragraphs: In conclusion, EHLC technology has the potential to significantly enhance the performance of cladding layers while simultaneously reducing costs through the advancement of cladding materials, optimization of process parameters, and the implementation of external field-assisted technologies. As technological progress continues and research deepens, the optimization methodologies for the EHLC process are expected to become increasingly refined. Accordingly, this paper outlines the following future prospects: Innovation and diversification of cladding materials: Encompassing not only high-strength alloys, heat-resistant alloys, and corrosion-resistant alloys but also functionally graded materials and biomedical materials. Exploration of intelligent optimization algorithms: Particularly in underexplored domains such as convolutional neural networks and radial basis function networks, with a concerted effort to develop hybrid algorithms that address the limitations of individual algorithms and enhance optimization accuracy. Expanding the parameters for optimization and enhancing the evaluation index system: This includes critical indicators such as the thermal properties, cooling rates, fracture toughness, and elongation of cladding materials. Development of a specialized online monitoring software platform: Utilizing real-time online monitoring data to achieve intelligent modeling and parameter optimization, thereby accelerating the research and development process. Diversification of external field-assisted technologies: Shifting from singular external field assistance to coupled composite fields, with a thorough investigation into the mechanisms by which these composite external fields influence the microstructure and performance of coatings, thus broadening the application spectrum of EHLC technology. Build a collaborative innovation system across the entire industrial chain: Through vertical integration of materials, equipment, and processes, establish a large-scale application demonstration platform to simultaneously reduce overall costs and improve the adaptability of EHLC technology to different operating conditions.
